references.text: The famine began to ravage all lands, but in all of Egypt there was bread. Joseph opened all the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians and to people from all lands. This is the direct background for why Jacob sent his sons to Egypt.
All lands came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, for the famine was severe over all the earth. This explains why Jacob knew there was grain to be bought in Egypt.

The famine was still severe in the land, and when they had eaten up the grain they had brought from Egypt, Jacob told his sons that they must go back and buy some food. This is a parallel to the first journey described in chapter 42.
Joseph explains that there have been two years of famine, and five more years will come without plowing or harvesting. This underscores the severity of the famine that drove Jacob to act.
When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there for the first time. Stephen's speech in Acts refers directly to the event in Genesis 42:1.
Direct narrative follow-up: Verse 7 shows the consequence of the event in verse 1 (the grain is used up) and continues the story of God's provision.
